To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) invariant representations are not always sufficient for successful domain adaptation and (ii) there is a fundamental tradeoff in the joint error of domain adaptation algorithms that learn invariant representations and that attempt to minimize the error on both domains.

(1) learning domain invariant representations is not a sufficient condition for successful domain adaptation; (2) the generalization upper bound for domain adaptation should explicitly take into account conditional shift; (3) there exists an information theoretic tradeoff between learning domain invariant representations and achieving low joint error on both source and target domains when the marginal distributions of the labels differ from source to the target; (4) our experiments corroborate our theoretical results.

1) learning invariant features alone is not sufficient to guarantee domain adaptation; 2) a generalization upper bound for domain adaptation that explicitly accounts for conditional shift is proposed; 3) an information theoretic joint error lower bound is proved that reveals a fundamental tradeoff in domain adaptation between learning invariant representations, and achieving small joint source and target errors; 4) our theoretical findings are corroborated with real world experiments
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of domain adaptation, where we have a labeled dataset from the source domain and a labeled dataset from target domain, but the target domain is different from the source domain.
the question: What is the best way to learn domain invariant features for unsupervised domain adaption?
the problem of learning a classifier from labeled data in a source domain and unlabeled data in a target domain, such that the classifier performs well on both source and target domain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the case of conditional shift, learning a representation that is invariant across domains is not sufficient for successful domain adaptation, and a more sophisticated approach is required.

1) the ability to learn invariant representations is not sufficient for successful domain adaptation; 2) the ability to achieve small joint error on the source and target domains is not necessary for successful domain adaptation (as shown by our counterexample).
the paper is a nice theoretical study of domain adaptation, with a very nice counterexample.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide a theoretical framework to understand the problem of unsupervised domain adaption.
we propose a novel generalization bound for unsupervised domain adaption and we show it is tight.

(1) the current state-of-art domain adaptation methods, which are designed to learn invariant features, are not sufficient to achieve a small error in the target domain; and (2) a small joint error on source and target domain is not sufficient for domain adaptation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
domain adaptation is a much harder problem than it is often believed to be.
domain adaptation methods should explicitly take into account conditional shift, in addition to marginal shift.
domain adaptation is fundamentally different from learning a good representation.
